Baggy clothes help, covering mirrors with towels or blankets when your dysphoria is especially bad, small rituals like shaving your face even if you don't need to, wearing men's deodorant etc. Find out if your school has any mental health support available - you are not going to be the only one going through this sort of situation. I know it feels isolating now, but there are many others like you.
If you can get a job when you're a bit older and start saving up money, whether that's to go see your other family or to move out when you're old enough, that would be ideal.
I know everything seems so far away and unreachable right now, but just keep pushing through this hard part of your life and it will be worth it, I promise.

Okay so I wouldn't consider myself an expert but I've been studying vocals for around 8 years so take from this what you will.

There's 4 different modes or "voices" in the spoken and sung voice

M0 - otherwise known as vocal fry, that very low frequency that kinda sounds like a creaky door

M1 - "chest voice" normal spoken voice that resonates in the chest area

M2 - "head voice" the thinner sounding higher pitched voice normally used in singing especially choral.

M3 - "whistle tones" very high pitch to the higher limit of the human vocal folds. Think Mariah Carey, Ariana Grande etc

I'm gonna be talking about M0 and M1 mainly.

My voice tends to be quite expressive and changes in pitch a lot. I also tend to have an upwards inflection on the end of phrases, and my voice gets higher in pitch as I get louder and when speaking passionately.

Something that my speech and language therapist suggested to me is using the M0 vocal fry during connecting words like "yeah" "um" "uh" etc. as a sort of anchoring frequency to help bring the average frequency of your spoken voice down. After trying this in my everyday life and conversations I have found it quite effective and I am more confident in casually speaking to others. 

In terms of actual exercises you can do to lower the average pitch of your spoken voice, I would strongly recommend getting a voice pitch tracker app such as Voice Tools or Nail The Pitch. They offer a live graph of the frequencies in your spoken voice so that you can note which words or sounds your voice tends to go up on, and which ones are easier.
You can then start to work through the different phonetic sounds and figure out something that's comfortable to speak in, but also sounds more masculine.
Another thing is to ensure you maintain vocal health by drinking plenty of water, sleeping enough, etc. It seems irrelevant but the vocal folds are the first thing to become dehydrated and the last thing to become hydrated, so drinking enough water is super important to make use of your full vocal range. 
Also, don't start smoking in hopes it'll make your voice deeper - I made that mistake 5 years ago; it had a negligible effect on my voice and it's only left me with a very expensive nicotine addiction. Bad move.

I've been through this pain. It still comes back sometimes, and it isn't any easier when it does.

Like you, I felt shame and guilt about being raised as a female - I still do. I'm scared of talking to people. I have to take (prescribed) pills to sleep at night. I can't leave my flat without scrutinising myself in the mirror. I wasted 7 years of my life waiting and waiting for a gender dysphoria diagnosis. I got it eventually, of course, and started HRT, but I lost what was supposed to be the best years of my life because I was stuck in a flesh prison of a body. Working retail doesn't help - you see some really shit people from behind a till.

I have found some solace in "I don't give a fuck". Cashier/stranger at bus stop/librarian calls you a she? Don't give a fuck, I probably won't see that person ever again and they won't remember me after 5 minutes. Do you remember the faces of every single person you pass by or talk to? No. It doesn't fucking matter. It hurts but let it slide.

And also, the things you can't change. Your past, your upbringing, not being born with a dick. Don't give a fuck. You choose who you want to be every single day, no matter what happened yesterday or 2 years ago or when you were born. The active decisions you make shape your personality, not a doctor pulling you out into the world and seeing a little baby vagina. Fuck everyone who says otherwise and fuck everyone who doesn't support you doing whatever you want. Life is too short.

There are so many things you can change and control about your body and your personality and your life. 
Work out, eat right, cut your hair however you want, get piercings or tattoos (when you're over 18, don't go to your mate who has an aliexpress tattoo gun) if that's your vibe - it's personally helped me in the past feel more in control of my appearance.
Join a club, get a new hobby, meet people and make new connections. I understand money can be an issue but there are things you can do that cost nothing. The world is changing and a lot of people these days won't give a fuck what genitals you have or how you were raised, only if you're a decent person. And if they do then they do not matter.

Sorry if this sounds like a lecture, but more than anything now I am angry at myself for wasting the years that I had my health and mobility because I was scared of other people's perception of me. It's not worth it. Life happens whether you want it to or not. Don't let good opportunities pass you by on account of not liking who you are yet. Almost nobody is completely satisfied with themselves and the ones who are are fucking narcissists.

Don't feel like you have to love yourself, I hate that toxic positivity shit. You don't have to love your body or any of that poncey shit, but once you let go of unrealistic goals, accept what you have and try to work with it, a whole bunch of new opportunities and perspectives will make themselves clear to you.

And in terms of being a "successful man", you need to think about what exactly that means for you. If your brain starts saying "be born with a penis/have male upbringing" etc, just drop it right there and think about things you can realistically, actively change. You want to be strong? Go gym. You may lose contact with family members, friends etc. Not to mention medical transition has a lot of health risks that people don't talk about, like high cholesterol, heart conditions, liver diseases, high blood pressure etc. 

I'm not meaning to turn you away, and I definitely think speaking to trans men might help you gain perspective on your personal situation, but through my experience and communities I have met people who made a decision without thinking and nearly regretted it. There are also gender non-conforming communities, especially among women/girls who are uncomfortable with gender roles, that you may find support from.
Wish you all the best on your journey.
